content: Swimmer's itch is a temporary immune reaction that occurs in the skin of humans who have been exposed to waterborne trematode parasites. The condition typically manifests as itchy, raised papules that appear within hours of exposure and generally resolve within a week. The condition was first described in Michigan in 1928 and has since been reported worldwide. The genera most commonly associated with swimmer’s itch in humans are Trichobilharzia and Gigantobilharzia. These trematodes usually complete their life cycles in birds. However, swimmer’s itch can also be caused by schistosome parasites of non-avian vertebrates, such as Schistosomatium douthitti, which infects snails and rodents. Other taxa implicated in causing the condition include Bilharziella polonica and Schistosoma bovis. Most cases of swimmer’s itch are caused by parasites that use waterfowl as their vertebrate hosts. These avian schistosomes are unable to complete their life cycles in mammals but can accidentally infect humans. This results in mildly itchy spots on the skin, which, within hours, develop into raised papules that are intensely itchy. These papules are caused by localized inflammatory immune responses, with each papule corresponding to the penetration site of a single parasite. The parasite dies within the skin within hours of penetration. For treatment, oral administration of hydroxyzine, an antihistamine, is sometimes prescribed to alleviate the symptoms of swimmer’s itch and similar dermal allergic reactions.
